chapter: Mente's factory, hard times and later life
title: Ten years working at the theater and the Social Security papers
summary: He describes his last job at the theater and keeping schedule tickets to settle his Social Security record.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: there and you never know them to play in no band. No musicians? I was working no musicians. He just got there. I think that's the picture there. Over there. Two tall fellas. They used to work at the theater where I worked at. I used to work at the theater too. The singer theater. Yeah, I worked there ten years. That's my last job I had. I had a time getting away from there. That fella had them all tied up, you understand? And I was working at that time piece, piece work. And every time he'd give me a... He said, Joe, I said, sir. He said, Joe, I said, sir. This fella by the name of Smith. Harlan Smith. He said, Joe, I said, sir. He said, yeah, I'll give you a schedule for tomorrow. I said, okay. He said, tear the whole one up. The fellas couldn't get away from him, you know. He had them all tied up. And what he was doing, he had them down for more than what they... He was paying them, you know. He was paying them, you know. Going south. Yeah. I said, okay. He said, tear it up. Tear it up. Tear it up. I'm going to show you them tickets. Some day you come here. I'm going to show them to you. And every time he told me, say, Joe, I got another schedule for you. Tear the one up. You don't need it no more. I said, okay. I said, I know I don't need it. I'm going to tear it. I got them all left. He saved them all. I thought, yeah. And boy, if I didn't keep them thing there, he'd have me there working for the governor a long time. I received a letter, you know, from the Social Security. And they told me, say, Ralph, I want to see you or you can write, telephone us or write to us. Do as you think better for you. I said, yeah. Took that long letter. Stuck it. Took all them pot times in my pocket.
What kind of work did you do? There was a piece work.

What is the theater? Oh, well, he had me there. You know, I didn't work all day like them other fellas, you know. Part time. Part time, yeah. And so, so, so, other while, he, he told me all the time, tear them up. Tear them up. You don't need them no more. I said, alright. I got them all the time. I got them all rolled up. And so, I got the letter from them fellas, you know. Told me, says, we wants to see you write or telephone us or anything. I took my time and all them papers put them in my pocket. Good thing you saved them. Yeah. You collect your Social Security now, do you? Yeah. Oh, yeah. And so, I had them all in the rubber. And said, Joe. I said, huh? You could have called me over the phone. No, I want to see you in person. I said, I want to see you in person. I said, I want to see you in person. I said, you messed up here. I said, you know. If you don't get this thing straightened out, you'll be working for the governor a long time. Just like that. I said, what's wrong? Well, the way things, the way Smith got you. He said, you'll be working for the governor a long time. I said, alright. I said, I want to show you something first. I took the people out. I took the people out. I had them rolling in the rubber. I said, you look at this. At other people and everything. A fella by the name of Mr. Wall sent me to this fella. And told me, say, Robinson. And I started away.
